title: OOP Basics: Classes, Objects, and Polymorphism
oneLiner: The same "compute a shape's area" problem, solved two ways -- one where adding a new shape means editing existing code, and one where it doesn't.
keyTakeaway: Polymorphism means calling code can work with ANY shape that satisfies the interface (the named set of methods every shape promises to provide) without knowing which concrete type it actually is -- a procedural if/switch (plain functions that branch on the kind of shape) has to be told about every case up front; an OOP design lets you add a whole new case by writing a brand new class and touching nothing that already exists and already works.
explanation:
Object-oriented programming organizes code around OBJECTS -- bundles of data (state) and the behavior that operates on that state (methods) -- rather than a big pile of standalone functions each juggling whatever data gets passed to them. A CLASS is the blueprint (Circle, Rectangle); an OBJECT (or instance) is one actual thing built from that blueprint, with its own state (this circle's radius, that circle's radius). ENCAPSULATION means an object controls its own state -- other code asks it to DO something (`circle.Area()`) instead of reaching in and recomputing that math itself from raw fields.

INHERITANCE lets one class build on another (a SavingsAccount could inherit from BankAccount, keeping its deposit and withdraw and adding interest on top) -- useful, but easy to overuse, and "is-a" in everyday speech isn't enough: a square IS a rectangle in geometry, yet a Square class inheriting a Rectangle with settable Width and Height breaks code that sets them separately (the Liskov Substitution trap in SOLID). COMPOSITION (an object HOLDING a reference to another object instead of inheriting from it) is often the better tool, since it doesn't force a rigid "is-a" relationship where a "has-a" one actually fits better. POLYMORPHISM is the payoff: many different classes can all implement the same method name (`Area()`) with completely different logic, and calling code that only knows "this is a Shape" can call `.Area()` on any of them without an if/switch checking which concrete type it's actually holding.

Compare the two versions below directly -- the procedural version has to know about every shape by name inside one function, so adding a new shape means editing code every existing shape already depends on. The OOP version's calling code never changes at all; adding a shape means writing one new, completely separate class. That property -- extending behavior without modifying existing, working code -- is worth its own name (the Open/Closed Principle), and it's the same reason this app itself can add a new lesson as "one new file," covered properly in Interfaces & Abstraction.
